---
title: "Interactive PCA Projection"
description: "Rotate a one-dimensional projection and measure variance captured and reconstruction error."
---

## One dataset, many projection directions

Take six invented orders, using only distance $d$ and number of items $n$. Their mean is $\boldsymbol\mu=(3.5,2)^\top$. After centring, consider a unit direction

$$
\boldsymbol w(\phi)=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\phi\\\sin\phi\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The one-dimensional score and reconstruction are

$$
z_i=\boldsymbol w^\top(\boldsymbol x_i-\boldsymbol\mu),
\qquad
\tilde{\boldsymbol x}_i=\boldsymbol\mu+z_i\boldsymbol w.
$$

The projected sample variance is $\boldsymbol w^\top S\boldsymbol w$, and total squared reconstruction error is

$$
E(\phi)=\sum_i\|\boldsymbol x_i-\tilde{\boldsymbol x}_i\|_2^2.
$$

For centred data and orthogonal projection, maximising variance **minimises** this error. Try rotating the direction and observe both quantities together.

## Rotate the candidate axis

~~~{ojs}
viewof directionDegrees = Inputs.range([0, 180], {
  label: "Projection angle (degrees)",
  value: 20,
  step: 5
})
~~~

~~~{ojs}
orders = [
  {distance: 1, items: 1}, {distance: 2, items: 2},
  {distance: 3, items: 1}, {distance: 4, items: 3},
  {distance: 5, items: 2}, {distance: 6, items: 3}
]
axis = {x: Math.cos(directionDegrees * Math.PI / 180),
        y: Math.sin(directionDegrees * Math.PI / 180)}
points = orders.map(({distance, items}) => {
  const x = distance - 3.5;
  const y = items - 2;
  const score = x*axis.x + y*axis.y;
  return {x, y, px: score*axis.x, py: score*axis.y, score};
})
Plot.plot({
  width: 660,
  height: 420,
  x: {label: "Centred distance (km)", domain: [-3.2,3.2]},
  y: {label: "Centred item count", domain: [-3.2,3.2]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "gray"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "gray"}),
    Plot.line([
      {x: -3*axis.x, y: -3*axis.y},
      {x: 3*axis.x, y: 3*axis.y}
    ], {x: "x", y: "y", strokeWidth: 2, stroke: "steelblue"}),
    Plot.dot(points, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "orange", r: 5}),
    Plot.dot(points, {x: "px", y: "py", fill: "steelblue", r: 4})
  ]
})
~~~

### Projected sample variance

~~~{ojs}
variance = points.reduce((a, p) => a+p.score*p.score, 0)/(points.length-1)
~~~

### Total squared reconstruction error

~~~{ojs}
error = points.reduce((a, p) => a+(p.x-p.px)**2+(p.y-p.py)**2, 0)
~~~

The orange points are centred observations. The blue points are their projections onto the chosen axis.

## Explain the mathematics

The covariance matrix for this small dataset is

$$
S=\begin{bmatrix}3.5&1.2\\1.2&0.8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For a unit direction, projected variance is $\boldsymbol w^\top S\boldsymbol w$. The best direction is an eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue of $S$, subject to the assumptions of classical PCA.

**Limitations:** the two features have different units. In a real dataset, standardising features might change which direction is considered most important. PCA finds variation, not necessarily predictors of fulfilment time.
